title: Japan's Tatami Mats Could Help Mood and Focus
paragraphs: Tatami mats have covered the floors of traditional Japanese rooms for centuries. Now, a new study from Japan suggests that the material used to make them may help people feel calmer and focus better.

The surface of tatami mats is made from a type of rush grass called igusa. In Japan, igusa has a distinctive smell that many people link with comfort and relaxation. However, according to the researchers, there has been little scientific evidence to support this idea. In addition, the use of igusa has declined as lifestyles and housing in Japan have changed.

The study was led by Associate Professor Kuniyoshi Shimizu of Kyushu University and published in the journal Scientific Reports in 2026. It involved 17 volunteers with an average age of 21.5. Each volunteer took part in the experiment twice, in a soundproof room. One time, they sat on igusa mats, and the other time, they sat on plastic mats with no smell. While sitting on the mats, they completed simple tasks. The researchers measured how quickly they reacted and recorded their brain activity using a method called EEG. Afterward, the volunteers answered questions about their stress levels and how comfortable they felt.

The researchers found a significant difference between the two conditions. When the volunteers sat on igusa mats, there was more activity in certain types of brain waves during the tasks. The researchers believe this shows that the volunteers were more focused and engaged. When the volunteers were resting on igusa mats, their brain activity also suggested that they were relaxing more efficiently.
In addition, the volunteers reported feeling less tense and anxious after sitting on igusa mats. However, there was no significant change in other aspects of their mood.
The researchers had previously found that the substances that give igusa its smell have relaxing effects. However, this study could not show whether the effects were caused by the smell itself.

The study also had some limitations. The number of participants was small and not very diverse, and only short-term effects were measured. Two of the researchers were also linked to a company that supplied the mats. The researchers plan to repeat the experiment with a larger group of people.
